replying_to: Replying to ePC: Overcoming Exponential Signal Decay in Deep Predictive Coding Networks
display_title: Official Review of Submission7533 by Reviewer wrgR

summary.value: This work proposes an alternative gradient flow procedure for simulating the convergence to the fixed point of (deep) predictive coding (PC) networks. To do so, this work proposes to, rather than optimizing over states (with a layer-wise locally defined loss, labelled sPC) to instead carry out an optimization to the energy minimum of a the errors at every layer based upon the global loss function (ePC). Experiments and figures demonstrate that indeed ePC significantly overcomes a delay in signal propagation which is inherent to the layer-local state-based optimization which is commonly carried out (sPC), while arriving at precisely the same equilibrium point. This allows significant increases in the speed of convergence of these models to the energy minima and the training of even deeper networks than were feasible previously.

strengths.value: This work is very well written and laid out. The set of figures and appendices are extensive and do a very good job of providing clear exposition of the problem at hand (signal decay within sPC networks). The contribution to the niche of predictive coding based learning is clear and could allow faster and more stable simulation time across the board. In fact, it may be that only an analytic solution for the errors in PC networks would allow for a faster measurement of the equilibrium point.

weaknesses.value:
This work suffers from a few significant weaknesses in contribution and in novelty:
1) Though this paper allows PC's equilibrium point to be simulated with greater speed and accuracy, it does so by removing one of the core and fundamental features of PC: that energies in sPC are computed at a layer-local level and do not require full backward passes to update. This work does away with that computation, in favour of a globally defined error at every layer which requires a full backpropagation operation at every timestep, and thereby almost entirely does away with the core conceptual purpose of energy in PC networks. I would therefore frame this paper as an implementational trick to reach the same fixed point as PC (assuming that ePC does not get stuck in some other local minimum or saddle point). Note that this change also means that this method can not be usefully applied for examining the dynamics of predictive coding (if one were interested in doing so). This weakness of this method and it's implications are little discussed in this work.

2) Atop issue 1, it is claimed in this work (section 6.2) that "ePC reformulates PC in a way that aligns naturally with digital processors, supporting efficient backpropagation and fast convergence across deep networks.". This is a very misleading statement and on the whole exhibits one of the key ways that the contributions of this work are misconstrued. In fact, the ePC reformulation could not ever be more efficient than backpropagation considering that it has no local dynamics whatsoever. The fact that every timestep requires a full forward and full backward pass (i.e. a full backpropagation step) means that this method is always as expensive as backpropagation in computation (and computational machinery) and could never be more efficient.

3) The two previous points also overall point to how the language used in this work is oftentimes overstated. For example, at the end of section 3.3 it is claimed that issues with the convergence time of sPC all end with "highlighting the need for a fundamental reconsideration of PC’s standard formulation." And in section 3.4 "ePC enables signals to reach all layers simultaneously without attenuation, while preserving the local weight update property that distinguishes PC from standard backpropagation." In effect, ePC does not appear to be a fundamental reconsideration of the principle of Predictive Coding (given that it is a trick for more rapidly reaching the energy minimum) but also the claim that it preserves local weight updating properties is rather disconcerting given that ePC carries out a full backpropagation pass at every timestep (the definition of non-local). Either ePC is an implementational trick (and therefore does not modify PC's core principles or takeaways and is a minor contribution) **OR** is a fundamental change to the proposal of PC (but therefore loses almost all relationship to PC aside from it's fixed point with much discussion necessary). It seems in this work that the authors do not choose a side and instead straddle this line claiming the benefits of both worlds.

questions.value:
If the reviewers wish to rebut the weaknesses outlined above, I would be happy to hear their opinions but am doubtful that I have misunderstood the core theoretical aspects of this work. I would be curious to hear:
1) How do the authors see this contribution if they had to choose a side? Is it an implementational trick with little to say about predictive coding? Or do they wish to claim a significant departure from predictive coding? It would be ideal if the text was rewritten to make this clear.
2) Given that these models can now be trained well and rather simply, how does performance scale beyond simple tasks like CIFAR and MNIST? It appears that if ePC is to have a major impact for deeper networks, the only case in which this would really matter is if it allows networks (like ResNet-18) to be trained also on more challenging tasks (such as ImageNet).
3) Given that PC was first proposed as a biological alternative to backpropagation, how 'deep' are biological neural networks and do your results have anything to say on whether this would suggest that sPC itself is unsuitable as an alternative to biological backpropagation?

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their explicit recognition of our work's impact on the field and for their kind words on our manuscript's form and clarity. We intuitively agree with the reviewer's instinct that it would be difficult to further speed up PC beyond ePC, though that is of course still speculative.

## Why non-local PC is still PC
The main obstacle for acceptance seems to be ePC's lack of locality, assumed to be a fundamental feature of PC.

However, it’s important to make a distinction between two separate lines of work that both go under the name of “Predictive Coding”:
1) In neuroscience: a description of cortical function (also referred to as “Predictive Processing”)\
→ Main property of interest: local, parallel, asynchronous communication
2) In Machine Learning (ML): a training algorithm, serving as an alternative to backpropagation and producing distinct learning behavior\
→ Main property of interest: the resulting weight gradients

For sPC, this categorization is merely a matter of semantics, as the algorithm belongs to both fields. For ePC, however, the distinction is crucial. We position our work solely in the second category, foregoing the first one. Our goal is to find PC’s weight gradients as fast as possible, which in turn implies performing the energy minimization process as fast as possible. We make no claims on biological plausibility, and locality is *not* a prime concern.

We agree that this may not have been entirely clear from our original submission, and have therefore fully revised the introduction to better reflect this.

To strengthen our case, we have also added a new appendix section (Appendix C.1) that explores a definition of PC given by Salvatori et al. (2026), and how ePC meets it.

According to this definition (which we agree with), PC's core premise is an iterative minimization of a variational free energy $E$ across a layered model. ePC does not depart from this premise in any way, even with its global graph structure. While Salvatori et al. consider locality a natural consequence of the definition, it is not: ePC meets all three requirements and hence is a non-local PC algorithm.

Along with this theoretical foundation, we agree with the reviewer that ePC also has significant practical advantages for speeding up PC research, which deserve greater emphasis. The 'fast' aspect of ePC is now better reflected in the paper's title, abstract, and introduction. Keep in mind, however, that ePC is more than an implementation trick: it is a theoretically grounded method, a direct reparametrization of sPC that maintains full equivalence at equilibrium, both in theory (Appendix C.2) and in practice (Section 4.3 and Appendix C.4).

The reviewer correctly notes that ePC cannot be used to examine PC state dynamics, which may be of interest to some. We have added this to our limitations section on "Different optimization trajectories" (L655), along with two citations of works interested in these dynamics.

comment.value:
## Rephrasing potentially misleading statements
The reviewer quotes three phrases from our work, flagging them as misleading or overstated. Please allow us to clarify and revise our words.

‎ 

> ePC reformulates PC in a way that aligns naturally with digital processors, supporting efficient backpropagation and fast convergence across deep networks.

The reviewer correctly notes that ePC could not ever be more efficient than backprop, and we touch upon this point a few lines further down (L533).

With the quoted sentence, we meant to say: "ePC is a formulation of PC that converges fast on digital processors. This is because ePC internally uses backpropagation, which is efficient on such hardware."

We suggest the following rephrasing to avoid confusion for future readers: "ePC reformulates PC in a way that aligns naturally with digital processors, relying on backpropagation to efficiently spread signals across deep networks."

‎ 

> highlighting the need for a fundamental reconsideration of PC’s standard formulation.

Again, the reviewer is correct to state that ePC is not a fundamental reconsideration of PC. It does not modify PC's core principles, which we consider a major strength rather than a minor contribution -- especially given the potential impact highlighted by the review's strength section.

The quoted phrase requires some wider context to be fully understood. There are many formulations of PC: sPC, iPC, hybrid PC, etc. A natural question is the establishment of a standard: which variant should people turn to by default? So far, sPC has been the de-facto standard in the PC community, and most other variants are built upon it (including iPC and hybrid PC). However, our analysis reveals that sPC has inherent flaws, suggesting that it’s probably a bad idea to use sPC as standard. Therefore, we call upon the field to look for a new standard.

We acknowledge this could be worded more precisely and have revised it to: "underscoring the need to identify a more suitable standard formulation of PC."

‎ 

> ePC enables signals to reach all layers simultaneously without attenuation, while preserving the local weight update property that distinguishes PC from standard backpropagation.

The reviewer makes an excellent point here. Upon reflection, we realize it is not the local weight update property that distinguishes PC from BP. An easy counterexample is ePC at T=1, which still implements local weight updates, but reduces to exact BP. Therefore, locality of weight updates is not a sufficient condition.

We have corrected the sentence to: "ePC enables signals to reach all layers simultaneously without attenuation.
Though no longer biologically plausible, ePC provably computes the same state equilibrium as sPC, resulting in exact-PC weight gradients."

Furthermore, we have revised several similarly-phrased sentences throughout the manuscript, shifting the emphasis from 'local' to 'exact PC' weight gradients, which is more representative of how ePC relates to PC.

comment.value:
## Addressing the questions

**Q1**: with respect to ePC, we see our contributions as follows:
- ePC is theoretically grounded and can provide novel insights about PC (e.g., Section 6.1)
- ePC is a much more efficient way of computing the exact PC weight gradients on digital hardware
- ePC moves away from the neuroscience view of PC as local-only learning, focussing instead on learning behavior, which is notably distinct from backprop (e.g., see Song et al., 2024; Innocenti et al., 2024).

Additionally, we view the analysis of exponential signal decay in sPC as another major contribution of this work, not to be forgotten.

**Q2**: we are glad to see the reviewer is fully embracing the effectiveness of our method and is eager to take it one step further. It is important to keep in mind that, before our submission, it was not at all clear whether PC was able to train deep models (even on simple tasks) -- an observation that led to a spotlight paper at ICLR just last year (Pinchetti et al., ICLR 2025). The goal of our work was to take up the challenge set by that exact paper, and as such, our experimental scope deliberately mirrors theirs (as mentioned in Section 5).

In a follow-up work, we would very much like to explore ePC's performance in even bigger models and more challenging tasks, ideally moving away from the setting of supervised learning where backpropagation is the undefeated champion.

**Q3**: this is an intriguing question, and it initiated a philosophical debate amongst the authors. Note, however, that our paper does not position itself as a neuroscience paper, and hence makes no claims about biology.

That being said, we couldn't resist engaging with this question.

It is very difficult to put a number on the 'depth' of biological networks. PC was originally formulated in the context of the visual cortex (Rao & Ballard, 1999), which consists of a couple dozen cortical areas spread across the 6 layers of the neocortex, and it remains unclear how 'deep' we can interpret this to be (Suzuki et al., 2023).

If we make the bold assumption of a depth of only 6 layers, we might say this is just about trainable with sPC, though it may require numerous iterations to reach state convergence. However, the brain is not iterative: it operates in continuous time. Therefore, another important question is: what is the time constant of biological neurons? And is it fast enough to uphold sPC as an explanation for biological learning?

The scope of the question can also be expanded to include neuromorphic hardware, where time constants are a simple design choice. Is sPC still fit for fast neuromorphic implementations? This too remains an open research question.

‎ 

## Conclusion
From the review, we got the impression that the reviewer really liked our work, but found a dealbreaker in ePC's lack of locality and a few unclear phrasings. The overall writing style and exposition of our work were greatly appreciated, and the contribution to our niche field was stated to be clear.

Therefore, we hope that, with the additional context and the significant edits made, including a fully rewritten introduction and an additional appendix section, the reviewer would consider increasing their support for this paper.

If the reviewer is not yet convinced of our work, despite the proposed changes to the manuscript, we will be happy to hear what the remaining hurdles are, to facilitate further discussion.

‎ 

---
### _References_
- Salvatori et al. (2026). "A survey on neuro-mimetic deep learning via predictive coding." _Neural Networks_
- Song et al. (2024) "Inferring neural activity before plasticity as a foundation for learning beyond backpropagation." _Nature Neuroscience_
- Innocenti et al. (2024) "Only Strict Saddles in the Energy Landscape of Predictive Coding Networks?" _NeurIPS_
- Pinchetti et al. (ICLR 2025). “Benchmarking Predictive Coding Networks -- Made Simple.”
- Suzuki et al. (2023). "How deep is the brain? The shallow brain hypothesis." _Nature Reviews Neuroscience_

I am responding here to the set of all comments made above. Please accept this response as such.

I appreciate deeply the authors' acceptance of criticisms that I leveraged against the framing of ePC, I think the changes make the paper more honest and clear.

On the other hand, I'm still troubled by the conflicting claims made by the authors. I now see ePC, even more, as being an implementational trick which is practically helpful but has little theoretical insight or contribution beyond the finding of the PC's fixed point rapidly. This saves on computational time, but has little significance given that PC is inherently guaranteed to be less efficient than alternatives (BP). The case in which PC is inherently efficient would be when it is applied in analogue hardware, at which point ePC would also likely be an unnecessary trick. This is not meant as criticism of ePC as a useful tool in the meantime, but meant as a note on the depth of impact that this work has and whether it therefore fits within this conference.

To further point at the confusing part of your arguments, at some point you say that the goal of ePC is the more machine learning one. That ePC is: `a training algorithm, serving as an alternative to backpropagation and producing distinct learning behavior.` However, by your own admission, (e)PC hasn't been shown as an effective alternative yet to backpropagation on anything more than relatively simple tasks. To be clear, I'd be willing to change my score if you were actually able to demonstrate the (e)PC is competitive with BP on tasks of some difficulty. My standard for this is training of models for classification of ImageNet. If you were able to show this, I'd consider that you have made a significant impact upon the field of demonstrating that PC networks are capable of this.

I hope these two points make my confused current perspective more clear. As such I shall keep my scoring as it currently is. I appreciate your constructive engagement very much.

summary.value: This paper identifies a critical flaw in Predictive Coding (PC) networks: exponential signal decay during the energy minimization phase, which has historically hindered their scalability on digital hardware. The authors propose error-based PC (ePC), a novel reparameterization that optimizes over prediction errors instead of neural states. This change enables global signal propagation via a backpropagation-like mechanism, resolving the decay problem while maintaining theoretical equivalence to standard PC (sPC). Experiments confirm that ePC converges orders of magnitude faster and successfully scales to deep architectures, achieving performance comparable to backpropagation where sPC fails.

strengths.value:
1. A primary strength is the paper's insightful diagnosis of exponential signal decay as the root cause of sPC's scaling limitations. This provides a clear, principled explanation for a long-standing issue in the field, backed by both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence.
2. The proposed ePC is an elegant reparameterization that effectively resolves the identified decay problem. By shifting the optimization from states to errors, the method preserves the core principles of PC while unlocking dramatic performance gains, demonstrating a deep understanding of the algorithm's mechanics.
3. The paper provides compelling empirical validation for its claims. The results demonstrate a significant speedup in convergence and show that ePC successfully scales to deep networks like ResNet, matching backpropagation's performance in regimes where standard PC is unstable or fails entirely.

weaknesses.value:
1. A key appeal of PC is its local computation, which aligns with biological processes. By incorporating a global backpropagation pass for error updates, ePC sacrifices this critical feature, making the overall algorithm less biologically plausible than the original sPC formulation.
2. The comparison is primarily against a basic sPC implementation. By not including stronger PC baselines from the literature that also aim to improve training dynamics, the paper may overstate the performance gap that ePC closes.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their kind words and are happy to see that the reviewer is as excited about this work as we are!

Specifically, we would like to expand on a few phrases that really stood out for us:

**"This provides a clear, principled explanation for a long-standing issue in the field"**\
We agree that a central contribution of this work is the diagnosis of _why_ PC has struggled to scale for such a long time. Since its early days of "PC can approximate backprop" (Whittington & Bogacz, 2017), the PC community has grown tremendously, with dozens of top-quality publications at ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS and Nature. Yet, many of these papers struggled with scaleability, necessarily and frustratingly restricting themselves to small-scale setups. Our work finally sheds some light on this mystery, identifying exponential signal decay as a core algorithmic bottleneck. And with ePC, that bottleneck is gone, enabling faster progress in the field of PC.

**"[T]he method preserves the core principles of PC [...], demonstrating a deep understanding of the algorithm's mechanics"**\
We appreciate the reviewer’s recognition of the design philosophy behind ePC.

When we first uncovered the signal decay issue, it quickly became clear that it was a fundamental problem, not of PC, but of its specific implementation as sPC. The question became: can we fix this, or is PC doomed?

Ending up at a solution as simple as ePC took a long time and lots of dead ends. But over time, an intuitive image of the solution began to form: an iterative scheme that alternates between forward prediction and backward propagation. Eventually, we converged to ePC -- its simplicity only obvious in hindsight.

**"[ePC] match[es] backpropagation's performance in regimes where standard PC is unstable or fails entirely"**\
This is precisely what we wanted to demonstrate. The work by Pinchetti et al. (ICLR 2025) revealed a major pain point of PC: networks that are perfectly trainable (proven by BP) fail to train with PC. Clearly, the issue was not architectural; otherwise, BP would have struggled too. The only possible conclusion: there is something wrong with PC. But what?

Our work provides not only an answer, but also a remedy in the form of ePC. The goal was never to _beat_ backprop (that would be far too ambitious), but to match it, using a principled PC algorithm. That is what ePC achieves.

## Contextualizing the noted weaknesses
**W1**: it's true, ePC is probably _not_ biologically plausible. We touch upon this point in our Clarifying Remarks (L682). In short, we argue for an algorithm-hardware co-design perspective: use ePC on digital hardware, use sPC on bio-plausible hardware. Denial is futile: sPC performs horribly on digital hardware (as we show in Section 3), and ePC cannot be implemented biologically.

We have revised our manuscript to emphasize this point more clearly across the manuscript, including in the abstract, the contributions, and the section introducing ePC.

**W2**: indeed, we only compare against sPC, not other PC baselines. This was an intentional design choice, which we clarify in our Clarifying Remarks (L673). In summary, Pinchetti et al. (ICLR 2025) already includes a vast experimental comparison of nearly all known PC algorithms, only to conclude: none scale to deeper models. In hindsight, this is not surprising, as all of these PC variants are built upon an sPC foundation -- a brittle one, that suffers from exponential signal decay, as we demonstrate in this work.

To further clarify our experimental design, our revised introduction puts more emphasis on the work of Pinchetti et al. (ICLR 2025) upon which we build significantly.

## Conclusion
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their encouraging and insightful assessment. Their remarks capture the intent of this work: to identify the fundamental scaling problem of PC and provide a simple, principled solution. 

We hope our clarifications and revisions have addressed the noted weaknesses, further convincing the reviewer of the soundness and relevance of our work.

‎ 

---
### _References_
- Whittington and Bogacz (2017). "An Approximation of the Error Backpropagation Algorithm in a Predictive Coding Network with Local Hebbian Synaptic Plasticity" _Neural Computation_
- Pinchetti et al. (ICLR 2025). “Benchmarking Predictive Coding Networks -- Made Simple.”

summary.value: The paper introduces error-based predictive coding (ePC), a reparameterization of predictive coding that optimizes errors instead of states, eliminating the exponential signal decay that makes standard state-based PC (sPC) impractical on digital hardware. ePC preserves PC’s local synaptic learning rule at equilibrium while using a global backprop-style pass for inference over the error variables, enabling fast, depth-robust convergence. Experiments on MLPs, VGGs, and ResNet-18 show near-parity with backprop and large gains over sPC in both stability and speed; theory clarifies when ePC collapses to exact BP and why it otherwise differs. The work reframes PC for digital hardware but in doing so foregoes some of the proposed advantages of PC.

strengths.value:
Pinpoints a discrete-time, depth-dependent signal decay in sPC and proposes a principled error reparameterization that removes it on digital hardware.


Shows ePC and sPC are equivalent at equilibrium yet follow different trajectories; specifies conditions where ePC=BP and warns against accidentally entering that regime.


Across deeper nets, ePC matches BP and far outpaces sPC in convergence (up to orders of magnitude), addressing PC’s well-known depth scaling failures.

weaknesses.value:
Weaknesses
Advantage over plain BP remains unclear: On standard supervised benchmarks, ePC ≈ BP in accuracy/throughput; the manuscript could better motivate when practitioners should prefer ePC to BP beyond the PC program itself.

Local/async claims need front-loaded clarity: ePC preserves local weight updates but gives up local/async inference (uses a global backprop pass). Make this trade-off explicit in the intro to avoid confusion with PC’s usual pitch. Note: this is also giving up on the advantages of PC.

The reparameterisation of Eq. 5 should not write yhat as a constant and instead make clear all the variables it’s computationally coupled to, ie yhat(x, e1, e2, …), as later stated in Section 4.2. The current writing mathematically implies that the gradients of Eq. 4-5 are the same.

 It is not clear whether the signal propagation analysis is as relevant after the first backward pass (or “wavefront”), since following from that the activity of any layer will be affected by both top-down and bottom-up layers. This point is supported by recent work by Ha et al. (2025). 

Related, overall it remains unclear whether the documented exponential signal decay is the root cause of the untrainability of very deep PCNs, or indeed why there should be only one main cause. Indeed, Ha et al. (2025) and Innocenti et al. (2025) identify 2-3 different pathologies of training deep PCNs. As an example, a vanishing forward pass initialisation can be equally problematic, even before considering the stability of the inference dynamics. So while exponential signal decay is clearly a problem worth investigating and sharing with the community, claiming that it’s the root cause seems an overstatement.

Ha, M. H., Sung, Y., Jo, Y., Kim, H., & Lee, S. W. Towards Stable Learning in Predictive Coding

questions.value:
Is this the “key assumption” stated in B.1? If so, this should be clearly stated and emphasised i the text.

What are the FLOPs, peak activation memory, and wall-clock time-to-target for ePC vs BP on VGG-9/ResNet-18? This would clarify practical trade-offs.

Can you include a small online/continual learning experiment (even toy) to showcase a concrete advantage over BP aligned with PC’s hypothesized strengths? The lietarure on this isn't convincing.
Please clarify in the main text (not only appendix) that ePC retains local synaptic updates but is not asynchronous/local for inference on GPUs/CPUs.

There is a rich deep learning literature about the signal propagation of the forward and backward passes of neural networks (e.g. Poole et al., 2016; Schoenholz et al., 2017). The analysis employed uses different techniques, and it would be useful if the authors clarified this while acknowledging the previously mentioned literature.

It would also be useful if the authors could discuss in more detail the relationship of their work to both Ha et al. (2025) and the ill-conditioning of the inference landscape recently reported by Innocenti et al. (2025). In particular:
Can exponential signal decay seen as a special case of ill-conditioning, since the former it’s a statement only about the first backward pass as pointed out above, while the latter is a statement about the entire optimisation process? In particular, ill-conditioning does not make the key assumption of Section B.1 (see comment above).

 The authors also state that architectural tweaks do not solve this sPC-specific decay (line 221). This seems to contradict Innocenti et al. (2025), who showed that ill-conditioning is a consequence of the feedforward architecture of PCNs and that conditioning (and therefore signal propagation) would improve for densely connected architectures. The authors’ signal propagation analysis clearly relies on this architectural assumption too.


References

F Innocenti, E Mehdi Achour, C. L. Buckley

comment.value:
We appreciate the reviewer's extensive evaluation and careful reading of our appendices. The review showcases a strong understanding of our suggested method: ePC indeed uses a backprop-style inference pass to make PC practical on digital hardware, without collapsing to exact BP.

## Improving clarity
The reviewer makes multiple helpful suggestions to improve clarity, which we gratefully incorporated in our revised version. In order of appearance in our manuscript:
- The phrase "the root cause" in the abstract was indeed too strong. We agree that several factors impact the trainability of deep neural networks in general, and accordingly, we have removed the phrase entirely, instead focusing on the hardware-algorithm mismatch of PC.
- The reviewer correctly notes that ePC sacrifices locality for optimization speed, and we have made this more clear in the intro and throughout the rest of the manuscript, including the abstract, the contributions, and the section introducing ePC.
	- As a sidenote, we believe that, in digital simulations, sPC does not hold any advantages over ePC. Its local-only nature is actually a major disadvantage (as shown in Section 3 and thoroughly analysed by Zahid et al. (2023)) and it is unable to capitalize on its parallel design (as discussed in our Clarifying Remarks, L691).
- The wavefront setting is solely intended to simplify the analysis and discussion. Overall, the signal propagation analysis remains valid for both top-down and bottom-up signals throughout the entire energy minimization process, and we have edited the text to reflect this.
- We have added to Eq. 5 that $\hat y$ is a function, not a constant.
- The key assumption stated in Appendix B.1 is only relevant (and necessary) for the approximate analysis of Appendix B, which stands separately from the main text. We have added a line to make this clear.

comment.value:
## Informal technical discussion
The reviewer raises several excellent technical questions (rephrased below), and we appreciate the opportunity to engage in a scientific discussion. It is clear that the reviewer has strong expertise in the field, with topics ranging from practical trade-offs to open problems and related work. Below, we share our current understanding on each, being transparent about what we know, what we've observed informally, and what deserves further investigation.

**What are the trade-offs between (e)PC and BP? When should practitioners prefer (e)PC over BP?**\
This is still an open question in the field, and we discuss it briefly in our novel introduction as well as our closing section (S6.3). In summary, there is some preliminary evidence of PC's learning advantages over backprop, but it's quite limited. We strongly suspect that sPC's scalability issues have hindered proper exploration, and with ePC, we hope to encourage further research in this direction. It is very clear that PC does something different from BP. The question remains: when is it better? And why?

As for the computational requirements: this depends on the exact implementation of ePC, and our research code is not sufficiently optimized for a fair comparison. However, from the algorithmic design of ePC, we can give some ballpark estimates (with $T$ the nr of ePC update steps):
* FLOPs: ePC ~ $T$ * BP
* Memory: ePC ~ 2 * BP
* Wall time: ePC ~ $T$ * BP

In the context of our experiments (supervised learning, following Pinchetti et al.; ICLR 2025), there is no known trade-off: backprop is better in every way. However, keep in mind that BP is our gold standard, and not some baseline we try to beat (that would be sPC).

**How does ePC perform on online/continual learning toy tasks?**\
We agree with the reviewer that the literature is currently not quite convincing about PC's performance for online/continual learning. There is a very real risk of overstating learning advantages based on extrapolated results on toy tasks. In fact, we currently have an ongoing project studying this exact setting, and we found that the situation is not straightforward: any advantages of PC depend heavily on the circumstances as well as the baselines used for BP.

Including a toy experiment may seem like a small ask, but without sufficient ablation studies around it, we’re just setting ourselves up for false preliminary conclusions. The setting requires a full rigorous study, worthy of a paper on its own -- and it’s coming up, so keep an eye out for that!

**What is the relation between your exponential signal decay and Innocenti's ill-conditioning?**\
Coincidentally, we had an informal discussion about this with Francesco Innocenti himself. He saw exponential signal decay and ill-conditioning as two sides of the same coin. Both imply a slow state convergence process, with the difference that ill-conditioning is a global statement, whereas exponential signal decay describes a phenomenon at layerwise level.

Ill-conditioning is a post-hoc measurement, a function of the weights that is fixed by the choice of architecture and algorithm. Our analysis of exponential signal decay provides more insight into _why_ sPC is ill-conditioned, with ePC solving the issue by applying a preconditioner (see L1200) that seems to enable efficient navigation through sPC's ill-conditioned landscape.

As clarified earlier, we would like to restate that exponential signal decay applies to the whole optimization procedure, not just the first backward pass (which served as an illustration to explain the problem). Informally, it can be summarized as: "In sPC, every layer traversal causes the signal to diminish." That is why we believe no architectural tweak can truly solve the issue: as long as there are layers, there is signal decay in sPC. Interestingly, Innocenti et al. (2025) found that residual architectures are actually much *more* ill-conditioned (see Fig. A.21) than standard layered networks.

**How does your analysis compare to a mean field theory approach?**\
We appreciate the pointers to the Deep Learning literature on signal propagation, which seems to use a mean field approach to estimate signal strength based on characteristics of the weight matrices. As noted by the reviewer, our analysis comes from an entirely different angle, and as such, it is very difficult to draw a comparison. Tacitly, we assume weight initialization to follow standard DL practices, which should avoid problems with vanishing or exploding gradients.

We are glad to encounter PC research exploring this area more thoroughly, and we have therefore added Ha et al. (2025) to our introduction as relevant related work.

display_title: Official Review of Submission7533 by Reviewer QnH3

summary.value: The paper demonstrates that standard predictive coding networks exhibit depth-dependent, exponentially vanishing error propagation in discrete-time implementations and proposes an error-parameterized variant (ePC) that updates prediction errors directly, achieving fast, depth-independent convergence while retaining local weight updates.

strengths.value: The paper pinpoints a very concrete, under-discussed failure mode of standard predictive coding—depth-dependent exponential attenuation due to discrete-time state updates—and reframes PC by reparameterizing over errors (ePC) to remove exactly that bottleneck.

weaknesses.value:
1. **Insufficient conceptual alignment with predictive coding (global backprop vs. PC)**
The proposed method explicitly constructs a global backpropagation pathway over the energy function to update the error variables, thereby propagating update signals in a backward manner. This departs from the core computational premise of predictive coding (PC), which emphasizes the propagation of prediction errors through purely local interactions between adjacent layers. Consequently, the method appears less as a genuine “reparameterization of PC” and more as “backpropagation expressed in PC notation.” The authors’ own remark further reinforces this interpretation, which suggests that the resulting structure effectively becomes a “fully connected (global) graph.”

2. **Violation of locality and resulting reduction in biological plausibility**
A significant source of credibility in the PC literature is the claim that synaptic/weight updates can, in principle, be implemented strictly locally. In contrast, the present approach requires, in its error-update phase, an explicit backward pass, along with a global control/broadcast mechanism. That is, the learning signal must be disseminated top–down in a single step; if this broadcast is impaired, the main advantage of the method—depth-independent convergence—no longer holds. This is not merely a modest deviation from the “spirit” of PC but a direct weakening of the PC narrative that learning can be supported by local signals alone, which makes it difficult to sustain strong claims of biological plausibility for the proposed variant.

3. **Questionable fairness in interpreting the performance gains**
Once global broadcasting of errors to all layers is permitted, achieving performance comparable to backpropagation is essentially expected, since each layer now receives essentially the same global supervisory information. Nevertheless, the paper presents these results as evidence that “PC can be scaled to deep architectures,” even though such performance is obtained by relaxing precisely those constraints (locality, limited top–down communication) that distinguish PC from backpropagation. To substantiate the claim that the work overcomes an *intrinsic* limitation of PC, additional experiments under identical biological and communication constraints to standard PC would be necessary. In its current form, the contribution can be read primarily as showing that “a backpropagation-like method labeled as PC attains backpropagation-like performance.” If adopted without such qualifications, this line of work risks diverting the PC community away from genuinely local and parallel formulations and toward methods that retain the PC label but are, in substance, closer to conventional backpropagation.

questions.value:
1. In the limit where the number of inference steps (T = 1), the proposed procedure seems to reduce to **one forward pass plus one global backward pass**, which is operationally indistinguishable from standard backpropagation. Do the authors therefore regard conventional backpropagation as a special case of predictive coding under their formulation? If not, what essential property (e.g., fixed-point inference, energy minimization over latent states, or particular locality assumptions) remains that would distinguish the proposed method from ordinary BP in the (T=1) regime?

2. The paper argues that introducing error variables and optimizing over them constitutes a predictive-coding-compatible reformulation. However, from an algorithmic standpoint, this appears equivalent to introducing intermediate variables solely to enable a **single global backpropagation over the inference trajectory**—i.e., to ensure that all layers receive the error signal in a single pass. In what precise sense is this still “predictive coding,” rather than simply backpropagation with an auxiliary variableization of the state? Could you please clarify the criteria by which you classify this as PC?

3. The proposed algorithm requires, for its global error update, that error information be **broadcast backward across all layers** in a coordinated manner. This implies the existence of a **global control or scheduling mechanism** that supervises what is a purely layer-local, sequential message-passing process. What biological or neurophysiological evidence do the authors rely on to justify the presence of such a global, backward-directed control signal? In particular, how would such a mechanism be implemented under realistic constraints on communication bandwidth, latency, and directionality in cortical circuits, and how does this differ from the well-known objections to BP-style weight transport?

4. In the special case where the number of inference steps is (T = 1), the proposed procedure can reasonably be interpreted as standard backpropagation—or, at least, as an algorithm that is functionally equivalent to backprop in terms of how error information is routed and applied. Suppose the authors nonetheless choose to classify this (T = 1) regime as a valid instance of predictive coding. Does this not amount to endorsing the view that human (or biological) learning could be implemented via a backpropagation-like mechanism? If so, could the authors point to concrete neuroscientific or computational evidence that supports the existence of such a globally coordinated, backward-directed, weight-relevant error signal in the brain? Conversely, if the authors do **not** intend to make such a commitment about biological learning, then it would be helpful to clarify the boundary conditions under which an algorithm should properly be called “predictive coding” rather than “backprop written in predictive-coding notation.”

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their careful and critical comments. The reviewer clearly recognizes the value of our problem identification (exponential signal decay in sPC) and the effectiveness of our suggested solution ePC.

It seems the primary hurdle for acceptance is the following question:
> **Is ePC still PC? Under which definition?**

## Contextualizing our work as ML research (not neuroscience)
Before we can address this question, it’s important to make a distinction between two separate lines of work that both go under the name of “Predictive Coding”:
1) In neuroscience: a description of cortical function (also referred to as “Predictive Processing”)\
→ Main property of interest: local, parallel, asynchronous communication
2) In Machine Learning (ML): a training algorithm, serving as an alternative to backpropagation and producing distinct learning behavior\
→ Main property of interest: the resulting weight gradients

For sPC, this categorization is merely a matter of semantics, as the algorithm belongs to both fields. For ePC, however, the distinction is crucial. We position our work solely in the second category, foregoing the first one. Our goal is to find PC’s weight gradients as fast as possible, which in turn implies performing the energy minimization process as fast as possible. We make no claims on biological plausibility, and locality is *not* a prime concern.

We agree that this may not have been entirely clear from our original submission, and have therefore fully rewritten the introduction to better reflect this.

## Why ePC is still PC
**W1**: the statement that PC's core premise is its local interactions is actually incorrect, at least in the context of ML. According to Definition 1 of Salvatori et al. (2026), PC's core premise is an iterative minimization of a variational free energy $E$ across a layered model, and we agree with this view. ePC does not depart from this premise in any way, even with its global graph structure. While Salvatori et al. consider locality a natural consequence of the definition, we show that it is not: ePC meets all three requirements and hence is a non-local PC algorithm.

We have added a new appendix section (Appendix C.1) to explore this definition and its requirements in more detail.

Furthermore, we would like to highlight Appendix C.2, which proves that ePC is indeed a genuine reparametrization of PC, and Appendix C.4, which empirically demonstrates that ePC is most certainly _not_ backprop in disguise.

We acknowledge that our original introduction may have overemphasized the importance of locality in PC as a learning algorithm, and we have rewritten it accordingly.

**W2**: PC's narrative of local learning is only relevant in neuroscience, not in ML. While ePC is indeed not biologically plausible, this is not a problem from the perspective of PC as an alternative learning paradigm.

For improved clarity, we have emphasized this point across several places in the revised manuscript, including the abstract, the contributions, and the section introducing ePC.

**W3**: we do not relax any constraints that distinguish PC from backprop, and we unambiguously prove that ePC is a PC algorithm (Appendix C.1 (new), C.2 & C.4). Note that ePC overcomes an intrinsic limitation, not of PC itself (because it _is_ PC), but of its digital simulation -- a crucial distinction.

As a closing thought, our hope is indeed to divert the ML-PC community away from local, parallel formulations of PC, which have significant disadvantages on digital hardware (see Section 3 & L691). As a digitally efficient PC algorithm, ePC is able to bypass the hardware lottery (Section 6.2) and use the prevailing hardware (GPUs, designed for backpropagation) to accelerate PC research.

comment.value:
## Answering the remaining questions
**Q1**: the reviewer correctly notes that ePC at T=1 reduces to standard backpropagation (as discussed in Appendix C.3). However, this specific setting does _not_ qualify as a PC algorithm, and we have added this important remark to our analysis. The essential property missing is a variational energy minimization procedure: $E$ must be at a minimum.

In that sense, both sPC and ePC implement PC if and only if $T\to\infty$. Of course, such a requirement is highly impractical for digital simulations, and the community has settled for approximate convergence in their experiments (see L157). Because of this, one might even argue that, under practical constraints, ePC is _more PC-like_ than sPC, because it will be closer to PC's full-equilibrium weight updates (e.g., see Fig. C.1, where sPC only begins to appear somewhat PC-like after ~200 steps).

**Q2**: so then, what _are_ the criteria by which we classify ePC as PC?
Our main criterium is that ePC produces _exactly_ the PC weight updates at equilibrium (theoretically proven in Appendix C.2, empirically verified in Appendix C.4). After all, in ML, this is our main property of interest. Additionally, our novel Appendix C.1 demonstrates how ePC meets the definition of a PC algorithm according to Salvatori et al. (2026).

**Q3**: we refer to the contextualization above: our method is not motivated by biological realism, but by computational efficiency, and as such, we make no claims on biology.

**Q4**: since we do not classify the T=1 regime as a valid instance of PC (a novel remark added), we believe this question reduces to Q1 & Q2.

## Conclusion

In summary, ePC produces PC's exact weight updates at equilibrium (Appendices C.2 & C.4) and satisfies the formal PC definition (new Appendix C.1). Our work focuses exclusively on PC as an ML algorithm, and therefore, locality is not our concern.

We have made substantial revisions, including a complete rewrite of the introduction and a new appendix (C.1) clarifying ePC's relationship to a more formal definition of PC. These directly address the raised concerns, which mainly pertained to the framing of our work.

Given that ePC provably implements PC weight updates and meets the formal definition, we respectfully ask the reviewer to reconsider the current score of 0 (strong reject). If the reviewer is not yet convinced of our work, despite the notable changes to the manuscript, we will be happy to hear what the remaining hurdles are, to facilitate further discussion.

‎

## Reviewers' original concerns & rebuttal summary
The reviewers also raised some concerns about our work, which we addressed in the rebuttal. We summarize the main points below, along with our responses.

‎ 

### **1. Biological plausibility** (QnH3, RUrq, wrgR)
Reviewers asked about ePC's lack of biological plausibility, a historically important aspect of PC.

**Rebuttal: clarified that biological plausibility is not our goal**

Our original introduction explained PC from its prevalent neuroscience perspective (local, bio-plausible), which was not entirely relevant to our work. Instead, **we fully rewrote the introduction** to better reflect our intended scope of PC as a machine learning algorithm, where weight gradients are the main property of interest.

Furthermore, **we added a novel appendix section** (C.1) to formalize ePC as an exact PC algorithm, despite its biological implausibility.

Finally, for maximal transparency, we explicitly pointed out ePC's lack of bio-plausibility across several places in the manuscript, including the abstract, the contributions, and the section introducing ePC.

‎ 

### **2. How does ePC compare to BP?** (QnH3, 4A7U, wrgR)
Reviewers wondered about the differences between ePC and backprop, and when to prefer one over the other.

**Rebuttal: in general, (e)PC ≠ BP, and some work finds PC > BP**

Appendix C thoroughly explores the link between ePC and backprop, establishing under which specific conditions ePC reduces to BP (an analysis lauded by reviewer 4A7U). Moreover, it demonstrates that, in general, (e)PC produces weight gradients that differ notably from those produced by backprop.

The design of ePC makes it inherently less efficient than backpropagation, which begs the question of when to use ePC. Our revised introduction puts **more emphasis on previously identified learning advantages of PC**. While those results are largely preliminary (as they were necessarily confined to small scales), ePC greatly facilitates further research into this area, at larger scales than previously possible.

‎ 

### **3. Clarity issues** (4A7U, wrgR)
Reviewers pointed out several phrases that could be worded more clearly.

**Rebuttal: addressed all reviewer-specific concerns and further improved clarity throughout**

We followed the reviewers' suggestions to improve clarity and preciseness throughout the manuscript. Additionally, **we revised the title** to better reflect the practical advantages of ePC **and tightened the abstract** to focus more on the essence of our work: PC faced a hardware-algorithm mismatch, and ePC fixes it for digital hardware.

‎ 

## Rebuttal outcomes
Reviewer 4A7U **raised scores (6 → 8)**, acknowledging a significantly clarified narrative of ePC as a digital PC algorithm, separate from biology. Additionally, the reviewer recognized how ePC could facilitate further research into the benefits of PC-based learning.

Reviewer wrgR also **appreciated the improved clarity** and **ePC's usefulness as a research tool**, but remained unconvinced of PC's learning advantages described in prior work, therefore maintaining a score of 2. The reviewer then indicated that a score increase would require an additional contribution: to be the first to **prove PC can train models on ImageNet**, a scaling not necessarily in model depth but in task dimensionality. **With only 6 days left before the discussion deadline**, we initiated ImageNet experiments but were unable to obtain conclusive results given the computational demands.

Reviewers QnH3 (original score 0) and RUrq (original score 8) did not reply before the discussion was frozen. Nonetheless, we hope that, like the two reviewers above, they too appreciated our clarification efforts. In particular, we believe that our novel introduction eliminates any confusion on the paper's scope (ML, not biology), thereby resolving the primary objections of reviewer QnH3.

‎ 

## Conclusion
We believe the revisions have substantially strengthened the paper. With one reviewer raising their score and another acknowledging improvements, it seems that the reviewers' original concerns have been largely addressed.

We recognize the challenge that the Area Chair faces without further reviewer discussion, and hope this summary may provide a clear, helpful picture of where the review process stands.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewers for their valuable feedback and commitment to a constructive discussion. With the new ICLR guidelines preventing reviewers from further reaction, we realize that the Area Chair faces a challenging task in determining the publication value of each paper. To facilitate the decision for our case, we summarize the review situation below.

‎ 

## Brief paper summary
Our work focuses on the digital simulation of Predictive Coding (PC), a machine learning algorithm distinct from backprop.

Our starting point is Pinchetti et al. (ICLR 2025), who observed two scaling issues:
1. PC is very slow, requiring lots of compute
2. PC struggles to train deep networks, even on simple tasks

‎ 

Our contributions:
1. **We provide a single mechanistic explanation for both scaling issues.** An important nuance emerges: the problem occurs not for "PC" as such, but for the _digital simulation_ of the _standard (state-based) formulation_ of PC. We demonstrate how this specific hardware-algorithm combination is a bad match, inevitably leading to signal decay and hence scalability issues.
2. **We introduce ePC, a novel PC formulation tailored to digital hardware.** Both theoretically and empirically, we prove that ePC is an _exact_ PC algorithm, producing the same weight gradients that standard PC would eventually return, while fully overcoming the signal decay issue.
3. **Empirically validated: ePC scales extremely well, both in time and in depth.**
	* We show that ePC runs orders-of magnitude faster (100-1000x in our experiments).
	* Copying the exact experimental setup of Pinchetti et al. (ICLR 2025):
		1. We reproduce the reported scalability issues of standard PC.
		2. We find that ePC leads to strongly increased performance, especially for deep networks.\
                Specifically, ePC matches the performance of backprop for (among others) VGG-9 and ResNet-18, trained on CIFAR-10 / CIFAR-100.

‎ 

### _References_
- Pinchetti et al. (ICLR Spotlight 2025). “Benchmarking Predictive Coding Networks -- Made Simple.” [link](https://openreview.net/forum?id=sahQq2sH5x)

‎ 

## Strengths noted by the reviewers
The reviewers highlighted several strengths of our work:
- A sound and strong contribution **(4A7U, RUrq)**, providing a clear, principled explanation for a long-standing issue in the field **(RUrq)**; a clear contribution to the niche of PC **(wrgR)**
- An insightful diagnosis of signal decay in PC **(RUrq)**; pinpoints a very concrete failure mode of standard PC **(QnH3, 4A7U)**
- ePC is a very effective solution to the PC scaling issue **(all reviewers)**
	- "ePC matches BP and far outpaces sPC [...], addressing PC’s well-known depth scaling failures." **(4A7U)**
	- "In fact, it may be that only an analytic solution for the errors in PC networks would [be faster]" **(wrgR)**
- Excellent presentation **(4A7U, RUrq, wrgR)** with an extensive set of figures and appendices that clearly explain the problem at hand **(wrgR)**

summary.value:
The reviewers were divided into the accept side and the reject side. I also carefully read this paper, and I recognize the strength of this paper: pointing out the exponential signal decay, a fundamental problem of PCs, showing systematic experiments, and proposing a possible route to overcome this problem.

However, I judge that the current manuscript does not overcome weaknesses that a half of reviewers pointed out. In particular, Reviewer QnH3’s point, “Insufficient conceptual alignment with predictive coding”, which means that the proposed algorithm lacks the locality of computation, seems crucial. Reviewer wrgR also raised the same question regarding the utility of the proposed non-local ePC. Actually, I also felt the same problem independently before reading their reviews. This mismatch fundamentally limits the contribution of this paper not only in neuroscience but also in ML, because in ML we can use the backpropagation algorithm, and it is still unclear in what tasks and hardware settings the proposed algorithm would have utility.

Unfortunately, this paper does not reach the acceptance line of ICLR and is evaluated as a rejection.
